claims.claim: Aggregate abundance change does not uniquely determine the direction of spatial reallocation.
claims.boundary: The systems and spatial scales differ; this is a qualitative falsification of sign-locking, not a pooled effect estimate.

claims.claim: The documented Ross acute breeding-state/access disturbance was followed by strong inverse-path spatial recovery.
claims.boundary: The inverse-path decomposition is post-result and does not identify individual returning birds.

claims.claim: Persistent Adélie decline at Palmer and Signy concentrated breeders beyond proportional thinning under the frozen count-error families.
claims.boundary: The analyses identify unequal attrition, not a single causal vital rate or movement mechanism.

claims.claim: Beaufort capacity release was associated with disproportionate growth of a small/new within-island unit and reduced movement toward Ross Island.
claims.boundary: Within-island census change and between-island movement are independent evidence streams; the census does not track individual movement.

claims.claim: Breeding-site fidelity can carry a recoverable spatial template after temporary breeding suppression.
evidence: Dugger et al. 2026 breeder movement <0.20% and common breeder-to-nonbreeder transitions
claims.boundary: No individual-level linkage connects the 1999 loss vector to the 2002 rebound vector.

claims.claim: Demographic turnover and capacity change can rewrite the spatial template future breeding expresses.
claims.boundary: The three classes do not share a common estimand and were classified after outcomes were known.

forbidden_promotions: process class significantly predicts a common spatial-reversibility effect size
short disturbances are reversible and long disturbances are irreversible
the same Ross individuals returned to the same breeding units
persistent decline necessarily causes irreversible spatial change
capacity release universally produces within-island spreading
the present synthesis prospectively confirms the process-dependent spatial-memory law
